title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We report a preregistered paired trial that measures whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single shared LLM generation per intent, deterministic verification, and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted verifier‑unsafe network changes relative to LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. Following preregistration (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N = 500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles using gpt-5-mini for generation and a deterministic network verifier for adjudication. Observed accepted final changes: baseline (LLM-only) 496/500; guarded (GVR) 500/500. Paired contingency: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The preregistered exact conditional two‑sided McNemar test on the discordant margin (n = 4, k = n10 = 4) yields p = 0.125. A predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates (one repair attempt per repaired task); total hosted model calls observed = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls), mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and bootstrap perspectives, document verifier semantics and known blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting semantics, present representative repaired‑episode diagnostics, and point readers to the archived evidence bundle and preregistration for full machine‑readable artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation from high‑level operator intent to device configuration promises large productivity gains for network operations, but generated CLI sequences that violate workflow or availability constraints can produce outages. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied for intent translation and AIOps, yet hallucination and factual errors remain primary reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A pragmatic architectural mitigation is generate–verify–repair (GVR): have an LLM produce a candidate canonical CLI sequence, deterministically verify that candidate against explicit workflow, dependency, and availability rules, and when the verifier finds violations invoke a constrained, bounded repair attempt. This paper reports a preregistered controlled paired experiment that asks: does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → at most one automated repair) produce fewer accepted verifier‑unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload?

We present an artifact‑grounded end‑to‑end execution (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) with N = 500 paired intents. Our contribution is threefold: (1) a preregistered paired trial executed end‑to‑end with frozen seeds and archived artifacts; (2) a detailed, evidence‑grounded description of generation semantics, deterministic verifier capabilities, and the bounded repair loop; and (3) reconciled inferential reporting that follows the preregistered exact conditional McNemar decision rule while also presenting the predeclared exploratory bootstrap interval and per‑episode verifier diagnostics for the repaired cases. We preserve the preregistered estimand, analysis plan, and all execution artifacts; numerical results below are reported verbatim from the archived analysis.
sections.related_work: The study synthesizes three related strands of prior work. First, recent surveys and systems papers document active interest in LLMs for intent translation, NetOps automation, and multi‑agent orchestration while repeatedly highlighting hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers; these works motivate tool‑augmented pipelines that embed deterministic validation as an operational gate [cited_record_ids]. Second, methodological proposals for evaluate‑and‑repair architectures emphasize standardized validator semantics, paired trial designs, frozen preregistration, and accounting for orchestration costs (model calls, repair attempts) when assessing safety improvements; these blueprints motivated our preregistered design and paired estimator choice. Third, deterministic and scalable network configuration verifiers have matured to check syntactic, workflow, dependency, and many availability properties at scale; however, verifier scope varies by which vendor or control‑plane semantics are modeled and thus which hazards are detectable. Our verifier implements canonical parsing, required‑sequence/workflow checks, availability/group constraints, paired‑field dependency enforcement, and final‑state comparison for the synthetic intent grammar—sufficient to detect the four repaired episodes reported here but deliberately limited with respect to vendor and timing semantics. The present experiment situates itself as a controlled, reproducible evaluation of a simple GVR gate using those verifier capabilities rather than as a claim about production readiness across diverse vendor environments.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 distinct intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). Sampling seeds, the deterministic task generator, and analysis executor were frozen prior to execution. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar on discordant pairs; an exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was predeclared as descriptive.

Generation, orchestration, and provider accounting: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model gpt-5-mini with fixed generation configuration. The GVR controller validated that shared candidate with the deterministic verifier and, if verification failed, invoked at most one automated repair attempt using the same model. The baseline condition accepted the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. Provider accounting in the archived run records model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls); stage_counts show shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4. Mean hosted model calls per accepted change is 504/500 = 1.008; for repaired pairs the observed model calls per pair = 2 (shared initial + one repair).

Deterministic verifier semantics: The adjudicating verifier applies deterministic canonicalization and a rule set to a normalized CLI sequence. Its pipeline includes: (i) syntactic parsing and canonical normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change patterns); (iii) availability and group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison with the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome. For each episode the verifier emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, a violation list and codes, and a boolean valid. A human‑readable codebook maps violation codes to descriptions; per‑episode verifier traces and diagnostics are archived with the execution artifacts.

Repair policy and prompt semantics: If the verifier fails the shared_initial candidate the GVR controller issues at most one repair prompt to gpt-5-mini using a constrained repair template containing (a) the original intent abstraction, (b) the verifier violation codes and short descriptions, and (c) an explicit request for a corrected canonical CLI sequence. The repair candidate is accepted only if the verifier returns valid = true. All repair invocations, repair prompts, and subsequent verifier traces for repaired episodes are archived and summarized in the results section.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and primary counts: Execution completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 1000; completed_pair_count = 500) with no failed episodes. Observed accepted‑change counts: baseline 496/500 (0.992), guarded 500/500 (1.000). Paired contingency counts were n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked in four episodes; each repair attempt produced a subsequent verifier PASS. Provider accounting: model_calls_used = 504 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 4).

Primary inferential analysis (preregistered): The preregistered exact conditional McNemar conditions on the observed discordant margin n = n10 + n01 and evaluates a two‑sided binomial tail on k = n10 with p = 0.5. For n = 4 and k = 4 the one‑sided tail P(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16; doubling for two‑sided yields p = 0.125. Under the preregistered decision rule (two‑sided exact conditional McNemar) this p‑value does not meet the confirmatory threshold and we therefore do not claim confirmatory statistical significance.

Exploratory interval estimate (predeclared): The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference was computed with 10,000 resamples and seed = 1729 and equals [0.002, 0.016]. The bootstrap procedure resamples paired observations without conditioning on the observed discordant margin; with only four discordants this exploratory interval can exclude zero when resamples repeatedly sample the few discordant favorable outcomes, but small discordant counts reduce frequentist coverage guarantees for percentile intervals. Because the bootstrap interval was predeclared exploratory, we report it descriptively while following the preregistered McNemar decision rule for the primary claim.

Repaired‑episode diagnostics (artifact‑grounded summaries): The four repaired/discordant pairs corresponded to verifier‑detectable sequencing or group/paired‑field dependency violations. Archived per‑pair verifier violation codes and short descriptions are reported here exactly as recorded in the validator traces:

- pair-000090 | violation_codes: [MUST_BE_DOWN_FOR_FIELD] — "VLAN/field changed while interface remained admin up; required 'must be down' sequencing violated." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000341 | violation_codes: [MAKE_BEFORE_BREAK] — "Backup uplink not enabled before primary was shut; violates 'make‑before‑break' availability rule." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000381 | violation_codes: [PAIRED_MTU_CHANGE] — "MTU changed on one side of a paired link without coordinating the paired interface's MTU change (paired‑field dependency)." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000413 | violation_codes: [GROUP_AVAILABILITY_CONSTRAINT] — "Both edge interfaces placed admin down simultaneously, violating minimum_active_in_groups availability constraint." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.

Representative per‑episode verifier diagnostics, normalized configurations, violation lists, parsed and required command counts, and the repair prompt/response transcripts for the repaired episodes are archived in the evidence bundle for audit. The numerical totals and contingency counts reported above are taken directly from the archived analysis results.
sections.discussion:
Reconciling McNemar and bootstrap outcomes: The GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted; these four correspond to the four discordant pairs (n = 4, k = 4). The exact conditional McNemar test conditions on the observed discordant margin and computes a binomial tail; with n = 4 the two‑sided p = 0.125. The predeclared exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero ([0.002, 0.016]) because the bootstrap resampling scheme does not condition on margins and, in practice, resamples repeatedly include the same small set of favorable discordant outcomes. Both perspectives are informative: McNemar enforces the preregistered confirmatory decision rule and is conservative under small discordant counts; the bootstrap interval provides an additional descriptive estimate of effect magnitude but requires caution due to small‑discordant count coverage limitations. We adhere to the preregistered McNemar decision rule for the primary claim while presenting the bootstrap CI as predeclared exploratory evidence.

Verifier scope, blind spots, and operational sufficiency: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. These checks are necessary for detecting many syntactic and workflow errors that LLMs commonly produce within our intent grammar and were sufficient to flag the four repaired episodes in this run. The verifier intentionally does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing and convergence effects, session/execution‑time errors, hardware resource limits, or subtle environment side effects; therefore a verifier PASS is necessary for experiment safety but not sufficient to guarantee production safety. Operational automation would require expanded verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, timing/convergence models) and live telemetry‑driven validation before unsupervised execution.

Operational implications and cost tradeoffs: Under the bounded repair policy observed here (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) the repair invocation rate was 4/500 (0.8%), producing modest additional model calls: observed hosted model call events = 504 (500 shared initial + 4 repairs). This low overhead in the synthetic workload suggests that a compact deterministic verifier acting as a low‑latency gate can materially reduce verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals at modest model‑call cost when baseline failure rates are low. However, realized benefits and costs will depend on baseline failure rates, verifier runtime at full inventory scale, how repair frequency scales under adversarial or more diverse intents, and the latency tradeoffs of higher‑fidelity verifiers.

Threats to validity and generality: Internal validity is supported by preregistration, fixed seeds, deterministic task generation, and complete execution accounting (complete_pair_count = 500; failed_episode_count = 0). Construct validity is limited by the verifier abstraction level and synthetic device templates; the verifier enforces encoded workflow and group constraints that match the synthetic intent grammar, but these rules imperfectly model vendor behavior and dynamic control‑plane hazards. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication, vendor‑specific parsing, and live telemetry tests are required to generalize. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08; the observed near‑ceiling baseline (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs and reduced realized power relative to the preregistered assumption. Together these limitations explain why a modest numerical paired difference appears in the exploratory bootstrap interval but not in the preregistered exact McNemar decision.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 produces an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016] while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification combined with a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in the studied synthetic setting; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated‑automation comparator which was not executed in this run. Archival artifacts including the preregistration, model configuration, raw results, per‑episode verifier traces, provider accounting, and analysis logs are available in the evidence bundle for independent verification and audit (see the prereregistered study identifier).

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. The generation model used in the archived run was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration). Key automated components in the run were a deterministic task generator, a deterministic network verifier, and a GVR controller implementing shared_initial_generation plus at most one automated repair per task. The study was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here are: N = 500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The immutable initial master prompt for this run is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt) and its SHA‑256 is 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and this revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this archived run; therefore the original preregistered multiplicity plan that would have adjusted for two confirmatory tests was not applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to the deterministic verifier’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation across two planned tests is not applicable to the present execution.
